newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU adopts rules to protect cross-border workers.
newsitem.headline: EU adopts rules to protect cross-border workers.

text.p: European Union employees who are sent by their companies to work in another EU state must be offered the same pay and working conditions as those hired locally, under legislation adopted on Tuesday.

EU social affairs ministers, after several years of debate, formally adopted the "posted workers directive", which aims to ensure that cross-border workers are not exploited and do not undercut local standards.
National governments have three years to turn it into law.

Agreement had proved difficult because of a conflict between countries including Germany, France and the Benelux states which wanted to protect their social standards and others such as Britain, Ireland, Portugal and Spain who wanted maximum flexibility for their workers.

The ministers reached a provisional accord in March, which was endorsed last week by the European Parliament, after the draft was watered down to allow governments to exempt some short-term workers from the rules.
Governments can wait for one month, for example, to apply minimum pay regulations to cross-border employees -- or allow trade unions and employers to negotiate such a delay.

They can also exempt "non-significant" amounts of work -- to be defined by them -- from rules on minimum wages and paid holidays and wait up to eight days to apply those rules to assembly and installation work.
In the latter case, the work would have to be performed as part of a service contract tied to the purchase of equipment and the exemption could not be applied to construction work.

In addition to pay and holidays, the rules apply to maximum work periods and minimum rest periods, supply of workers by temporary employment agencies, health and safety standards and protection of pregnant women and young people.
Britain, which argued that the text was too restrictive and included so many exemptions it would only confuse employers, voted against the legislation.
Portugal, a big exporter of construction labour, abstained, complaining that the text included stricter rules for that sector than for others.
